title: Discovering Spirits: China
text:
Spirits in Chinese classical and medieval texts do not coalesce into a single, uniform pantheon or reflect a static national essence. Instead, textual witnesses present contrasting structures of encounter, sovereignty, and moral reckoning. Rather than an evolutionary sequence running from wild animism to imperial bureaucracy, the surviving literature records distinct relational models: geographic distance crossed by mortal longing, elusive vegetal presence fractured by doubt, sovereign opacity governing cosmic cycles, and rigorous somatic surveillance tallying ethical debt.
In this issue, we examine three profiles through six primary source passages registered across pre-Qin and Song dynasty traditions, distinguishing primary evidence from later reception and editorial inference.

title: Discovering Spirits: China
section: Profile 1: Xiwangmu (西王母) — Fangs and the Distance of Return
text:
Profile 1: Xiwangmu (西王母) — Fangs and the Distance of Return

Who and How Known
The Queen Mother of the West appears across contrasting early corpora. In the Shanhaijing, she is depicted as a feral, theriomorphic figure presiding over jade peaks: > 西王母其狀如人豹尾虎齒而善嘯蓬髮戴勝 > > “The Queen Mother of the West has a human form, a leopard’s tail and tiger’s teeth, is skilled at whistling, and wears dishevelled hair and a sheng headdress.” (source-206, Shanhaijing juan 2, Siku recension)
In Mu Tianzi Zhuan, however, she appears as an interlocutor exchanging formal verse with King Mu of Zhou at the Turquoise Pond: > 白雲在天，丘陵自出。道裡悠遠，山川間之 〈 間音諫 〉 ，將子無死 〈 將，請也 〉 ，尚能複來 > > “White clouds are in heaven; hills emerge of themselves. The road is distant, mountains and rivers divide us. May you not die, and still be able to return.” (source-211, Mu Tianzi Zhuan juan 3)


What She Commands
Neither passage records a formal divine commandment or theological dogma. The Shanhaijing entry describes an uncanny form without issuing moral orders. In Mu Tianzi Zhuan, Xiwangmu’s song voices a conditional plea: survival across distance and mortality (將子無死，尚能複來). It does not confer immortality upon the king.


Where to Learn
Study the retained witnesses: the Shanhaijing (玉山 entry) and Mu Tianzi Zhuan (juan 3). Guo Pu’s Jin-dynasty commentary explicitly bridges these traditions by quoting the king’s narrative, illustrating editorial reception rather than prehistoric unity.

title: Discovering Spirits: China
section: Profile 2: Shan Gui (山鬼) — Vegetal Presence and the Incursion of Doubt
text:
Profile 2: Shan Gui (山鬼) — Vegetal Presence and the Incursion of Doubt

Who and How Known
In the Chuci (Jiu Ge), the mountain spirit is perceived through shifting sensory contours within southern Chu poetry: > 若有人兮山之阿，被薜荔兮帶女羅。 > > “As if someone were in the mountain’s recess, clothed in creeping fig and girdled with nüluo.” (source-230, Jiu Ge, line 1)
The spirit’s existence is anchored in mountain springs and flora, yet the communion fractures into hesitation: > 山中人兮芳杜若，飲石泉兮蔭松柏，君思我兮然疑作。 > > “The mountain person is fragrant with duruo, drinks from stone springs and shelters beneath pine and cypress; you think of me—yet doubt arises.” (source-232, Jiu Ge, line 11)


What She Commands
The text articulates no legislative command. Instead, an expectation of reciprocal attention is inferred through the poetic voice. The consumption of stone springs and wild herbs depicts wild sustenance rather than an institutional ascetic discipline. Rival readings interpret the figure as a local mountain numen in liturgical drama, an erotic persona, or a political allegory of the estranged minister.


Where to Learn
Read the Jiu Ge witness preserved in the Chuci collection. The unstable speaker identities reflect southern ritual poetry preserved through Han editorial collation.

title: Discovering Spirits: China
section: Profile 3: Da Siming (大司命) and Lifespan Accounting
text:
Profile 3: Da Siming (大司命) and Lifespan Accounting

Who and How Known
In the Chu hymns, Da Siming embodies sovereign cosmic opacity, operating beyond human comprehension: > 壹陰兮壹陽，衆莫知兮余所為。 > > “Now yin, now yang; the multitude does not know what I do.” (source-251, Jiu Ge, line 8)
By the Song dynasty, popular morality texts such as the Taishang Ganying Pian transpose destiny into internal somatic and domestic surveillance: > 又有三尸神，在人身中，每到庚申日，輒上詣天曹，言人罪過。月晦之日，竈神亦然。凡人有過，大則奪紀，小則奪算。 > > “There are also Three Corpse-Spirits within people’s bodies. On every gengshen day they ascend to Heaven’s bureau and report people’s transgressions. At month’s end the Kitchen God does likewise. Major offences subtract ji, minor ones suan.” (source-233, Taishang Ganying Pian)


What They Command
While Da Siming withholds the logic of divine action, the Taishang Ganying Pian commands rigorous ethical self-examination. Transgressions trigger explicit deductions of life allotments (ji and suan). Avoidance of wrongdoing is commanded for those seeking longevity, framing spirits as celestial recording officers.


Where to Learn
Examine the Jiu Ge hymn alongside Song morality literature (shanshu). This juxtaposition illustrates an analogical tension between cosmic inscrutability and forensic moral bookkeeping.

title: Corrections and Critical Distinctions
text:
In reconstructing early Chinese spirits, it is vital to separate demonstrable textual transmission from retrospective thematic analogy:

Documented Transmission (connection-370):

Claim: The Jin commentary attributed to Guo Pu in the Shanhaijing (Xi Shan Jing, 玉山 entry; source-206 / source-d1c1a82fd25723dd) explicitly quotes Mu Tianzi Zhuan (source-211 / source-0fdb8e80114f46bd), citing Xiwangmu’s Turquoise Pond song.
Boundary & Limits: This establishes reception by a Jin commentator, not textual transmission between the pre-Qin root compositions. The citation differs slightly in character choices (山陵 vs. 丘陵, 尚復能來 vs. 尚能複來). It does not demonstrate historical encounter, nor does it establish that the feral mountain ruler evolved into the courtly host.

Poetic & Relational Analogy (connection-372):

Mu Tianzi Zhuan (source-211) and Shan Gui (source-230, source-232) both articulate encounters predicated on absence, distance, and fragility.
Limits: This structural similarity does not prove historical influence or common liturgy. Mu Tianzi Zhuan stages an encounter between named courtly figures, whereas Shan Gui presents an unstable poetic persona whose gender and address remain ambiguous.

Cosmic Opacity vs. Forensic Surveillance (connection-374):

Da Siming (source-251) asserts divine opacity (衆莫知兮余所為), whereas Taishang Ganying Pian (source-233) details an inner-body surveillance apparatus (Three Corpse-Spirits, Kitchen God) docking life allotments.
Limits: While later supplements cite Siming docking ji and suan, this does not demonstrate identity with the Chu deity Da Siming. Moral pedagogy and cosmic opacity operate in tension, not logical contradiction.

title: Corrections and Critical Distinctions
text:
Textual Corrections & Provenance Adjustments

Dating of Mu Tianzi Zhuan (source-211): The 279 CE Western Jin date designates the recovery of the bamboo slips from the Jizhong tomb, not the composition or burial date (c. 4th century BCE). Surviving electronic texts reflect post-recovery editorial collations.
Botanical Identifications in Shan Gui (source-230, source-232): Terms such as pili (薜荔, creeping fig), nüluo (女羅, dodder / usnea), and duruo (杜若, pollia / ginger-lily) are provisional identifications in early southern flora.
Allegorical Flattening: Han commentary (Wang Yi) interpreted the Jiu Ge as direct political allegory of a rejected minister. We preserve the text as evidence of ritual dramatic poetry without asserting that commentary exhausted its primary significance.
Units of Deduction in Taishang Ganying Pian (source-233): The terms ji (紀) and suan (算) are kept untranslated. Numerical equivalences (e.g., 12 years or 100 days) derive from later commentaries and are not specified in the primary passage itself.

title: Annotated Library
text:
This library documents the six primary source citations supporting the Discovering Spirits: China issue. English renderings are provisional translations by Ada, unless noted. Original classical texts, recensions, locators, and critical limitations are recorded below.


Profile 1: Xiwangmu (西王母)

1. Feral Manifestation — source-206

Author / Attribution: Anonymous (with commentary attributed to Guo Pu / 郭璞, Jin dynasty).
Work & Locator: Shanhaijing (山海經), Juan 2 (Xi Shan Jing / 西次三經), 玉山 entry.
Edition: Wenyuange Siku Quanshu recension (欽定四庫全書本), retained evidence source-d1c1a82fd25723dd.
Date: Compilation broadly dated Warring States to Han; commentary c. 310–324 CE; Siku imperial recension is 18th century.
Exact Passage: > 西王母其狀如人豹尾虎齒而善嘯蓬髮戴勝
Provisional Rendering: “The Queen Mother of the West has a human form, a leopard’s tail and tiger’s teeth, is skilled at whistling, and wears dishevelled hair and a sheng headdress.”
Limitations: Preserved via late imperial court compilation; base text and Jin commentary are collated together.



2. The King Mu Exchange — source-211

Author / Attribution: Anonymous; recovered from Jizhong tomb cache in 279 CE; annotated by Guo Pu.
Work & Locator: Mu Tianzi Zhuan (穆天子傳), Juan 3, 乙丑 (yichou) day entry.
Edition: Sibu Congkan / Wikisource electronic witness, retained evidence source-0fdb8e80114f46bd.
Date: Warring States burial context; recovered 279 CE (Western Jin). Recovery date is not burial or composition date.
Exact Passage (with glosses): > 白雲在天，丘陵自出。道裡悠遠，山川間之 〈 間音諫 〉 ，將子無死 〈 將，請也 〉 ，尚能複來
Provisional Rendering: “White clouds are in heaven; hills emerge of themselves. The road is distant, mountains and rivers divide us. May you not die, and still be able to return.”
Limitations: Reconstructed from damaged 3rd-century tomb bamboo slips; print ancestry unverified; reflects Jin editorial reconstructions.





Profile 2: Shan Gui (山鬼)

3. Vegetal Cloaking — source-230

Author / Attribution: Qu Yuan (屈原, attr.).
Work & Locator: Chuci (楚辭), Jiu Ge (九歌), section 9: 山鬼 (Shan Gui), line 1.
Edition: Wikisource recension, retained evidence source-222bb81db340d668.
Date: Warring States period (c. 3rd century BCE).
Exact Passage: > 若有人兮山之阿，被薜荔兮帶女羅。
Provisional Rendering: “As if someone were in the mountain’s recess, clothed in creeping fig and girdled with nüluo.”
Limitations: Botanical determinations are provisional. Han allegorical commentary (Wang Yi) filters early ritual context.



4. Sustenance and Doubt — source-232

Author / Attribution: Qu Yuan (屈原, attr.).
Work & Locator: Chuci (楚辭), Jiu Ge (九歌), section 9: 山鬼 (Shan Gui), line 11.
Edition: Wikisource recension, retained evidence source-222bb81db340d668.
Date: Warring States period (c. 3rd century BCE).
Exact Passage: > 山中人兮芳杜若，飲石泉兮蔭松柏，君思我兮然疑作。
Provisional Rendering: “The mountain person is fragrant with duruo, drinks from stone springs and shelters beneath pine and cypress; you think of me—yet doubt arises.”
Limitations: Speaker attribution and grammatical subject of doubt (ran yi zuo) remain contested among commentators.





Profile 3: Da Siming & Lifespan Accounting

5. Sovereign Opacity — source-251

Author / Attribution: Qu Yuan (屈原, attr.).
Work & Locator: Chuci (楚辭), Jiu Ge (九歌), section 3: 大司命 (Da Siming), line 8.
Edition: Wikisource recension, retained evidence source-222bb81db340d668.
Date: Warring States period (c. 3rd century BCE).
Exact Passage: > 壹陰兮壹陽，衆莫知兮余所為。
Provisional Rendering: “Now yin, now yang; the multitude does not know what I do.”
Limitations: Astrological liturgy of Chu; textual survival shaped by Western Han compilers.



6. Somatic Surveillance & Lifespan Deductions — source-233

Author / Attribution: Anonymous (attributed to Taishang Laojun).
Work & Locator: Taishang Ganying Pian (太上感應篇), opening section.
Edition: Daozang / popular morality book tradition, retained evidence source-6c9358eff3cd56d1.
Date: Song dynasty (c. 12th century CE).
Exact Passage: > 又有三尸神，在人身中，每到庚申日，輒上詣天曹，言人罪過。月晦之日，竈神亦然。凡人有過，大則奪紀，小則奪算。
Provisional Rendering: “There are also Three Corpse-Spirits within people’s bodies. On every gengshen day they ascend to Heaven’s bureau and report people’s transgressions. At month’s end the Kitchen God does likewise. Major offences subtract ji, minor ones suan.”
Limitations: Generic Daozang / shanshu print ancestry is uncollated. Units ji (紀) and suan (算) are retained untranslated; specific temporal quantities represent later commentary.
